title: Defect Management
concept:
**Defect management** is the lifecycle process of handling defects from discovery to closure. The CTFL syllabus emphasises consistent, evidence-based handling.

**Defect lifecycle (typical states)**: New → Open (assigned) → In Progress → Fixed → Re-test → Verified → Closed. Branches: Rejected (not a defect), Deferred (won't fix this release), Duplicate.

**Defect report contents**:
- Unique ID.
- Title (short, descriptive).
- Severity (impact on system / users): blocker, critical, major, minor, trivial.
- Priority (urgency to fix): often separate from severity.
- Steps to reproduce (deterministic, ideally with screenshots / logs).
- Expected vs actual behaviour.
- Environment (OS, browser, build version).
- Test case reference (if any).
- Reporter and assignee.
- Status and history.

**Severity vs Priority**: Severity is product-impact; priority is business-urgency. A blocker severity defect in an unused feature may have low priority; a minor cosmetic defect on the homepage may have high priority because every visitor sees it.

**Defect triage**: a periodic meeting (often daily in late testing) where stakeholders review open defects, assign severity/priority, and decide fix-now / fix-later / defer / reject.

Good defect reports save time, drive fix prioritisation, and feed root-cause analysis. Bad reports ('it doesn't work') generate back-and-forth and miss the fix window.
keyPoints: Defect lifecycle: New → Open → In Progress → Fixed → Re-test → Verified → Closed; plus Rejected, Deferred, Duplicate.
Good defect reports include reproducible steps, expected vs actual, environment, severity, priority.
Severity (impact) and priority (urgency) are distinct — a severe defect in an unused feature may have low priority.

quiz.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes severity from priority of a defect?
options: Severity and priority are two names for the same property.
Severity measures the impact on the system or users; priority measures the urgency to fix.
Severity is set by developers; priority is set by testers.
Severity always equals priority for blocker defects.
quiz.explanation: Severity is about *impact*; priority is about *urgency*. A blocker severity defect in a rarely-used feature may have low priority (defer it). A minor severity defect on the home page may have high priority (every visitor sees it). The two are independent and both are assigned by the team during triage.
